prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

An optical aperture multiplier includes a first optical waveguide (10) having a rectangular cross-section and including partially reflecting surfaces (40) at an oblique angle to a direction of elongation of the waveguide. A second optical waveguide (20), also including partially reflecting surfaces (45) at an oblique angle, is optically coupled with the first optical waveguide (10). An image coupled into the first optical waveguide with an initial direction of propagation at an oblique coupling angle advances by four-fold internal reflection along the first optical waveguide, with a proportion of intensity of the image reflected at the partially reflecting surfaces so as to be coupled into the second optical waveguide, and then propagates through two-fold reflection within the second optical waveguide, with a proportion of intensity of the image reflected at the partially reflecting surfaces so as to be directed outwards from one of the parallel faces as a visible image.

The optical aperture multiplier is constructed from two rectangular waveguides that are optically coupled to one another. Each waveguide extends along a defined direction of elongation and contains a set of partially reflecting surfaces arranged at oblique angles relative to that direction. These angled reflective surfaces are used to control the propagation and extraction of image light within the system.

During operation, an image is introduced into the first waveguide at an oblique coupling angle. Once inside, the image light propagates along the first waveguide by means of four-fold internal reflection, allowing the optical information to travel through the guide while maintaining the desired image characteristics. As the light encounters the partially reflecting surfaces within the first waveguide, a portion of the image intensity is redirected out of the first waveguide and coupled into the second waveguide.

After entering the second waveguide, the image continues to propagate by two-fold internal reflection. The partially reflecting surfaces in the second waveguide then direct the image light outward from the structure. In this way, the system multiplies or expands the effective optical aperture and presents the extracted light to an observer as a visible image.

An optical aperture multiplier is an optical device designed to increase the effective viewing aperture through which an image can be observed. It includes two rectangular optical waveguides that are optically coupled to one another so that image-bearing light introduced into the device can be transferred from one waveguide to the other while maintaining the image information. Each waveguide has reflective internal surfaces that guide the light by total internal reflection, allowing the image to propagate along the length of the structure without requiring a correspondingly large input aperture.

Within the waveguides are a series of obliquely angled partially reflecting surfaces. These surfaces are positioned at selected angles relative to the longitudinal axes of the waveguides so that, as the image light travels through the device, portions of the light are repeatedly redirected. Some of the light continues to propagate internally, while other portions are reflected outward toward an observer. In this way, the device gradually extracts image intensity at multiple locations along the waveguides rather than emitting the entire image at a single point.

The first waveguide may receive the input image and distribute it through a staged sequence of internal reflections. In one stage, the light follows a four-fold reflection path, causing the image information to be replicated or spread across an expanded aperture in one direction. The redirected light is then coupled into the second waveguide, where a further staged reflection process occurs. In this second stage, the light may follow a two-fold reflection path, expanding or redirecting the aperture in another direction and allowing the output image to be presented over a larger viewing region.

Because the partially reflecting surfaces extract only selected portions of the propagating light at each interaction, the image can be made visible across an extended output area while preserving the spatial content of the original input image. The sequential combination of the four-fold and two-fold reflection paths enables compact aperture expansion without the need for a bulky conventional optical system. Such an arrangement is useful in applications where a small image source must be presented through a larger apparent viewing aperture, including near-eye displays, head-mounted displays, and other compact imaging systems.
outputs.L5:
An optical aperture is an opening or hole through which light passes in an optical system. It is an essential part of devices such as cameras, microscopes, telescopes, and projectors. The aperture controls the amount of light that enters the system and influences the quality of the image produced.

In photography, the aperture is usually found inside the camera lens. It can be adjusted to become wider or narrower. A larger aperture allows more light to reach the camera sensor, which is useful in dark conditions. A smaller aperture lets in less light, but it can make more of the image appear sharp and in focus. This effect is known as depth of field.

Optical apertures also affect resolution and diffraction. If an aperture is too small, light waves bend around its edges, causing diffraction and reducing image sharpness. If it is too large, optical imperfections in the lens may become more noticeable. For this reason, optical systems are designed carefully to balance brightness, sharpness, and clarity.

In scientific instruments, apertures help control light paths and reduce unwanted stray light. In telescopes, the size of the aperture determines how much light the instrument can collect. A larger telescope aperture can capture fainter objects and reveal more detail in stars, planets, and galaxies.

Overall, an optical aperture plays a vital role in managing light. By controlling brightness, focus, and image quality, it helps optical instruments produce clearer and more useful images.

Light coupled into the first waveguide is propagated by internal reflections and is partially redirected by the oblique surfaces to provide aperture expansion in a first direction. At least a portion of the redirected light is coupled into the second waveguide, in which further propagation by internal reflections and interaction with the oblique partially reflecting surfaces provides aperture expansion in a second direction, different from the first direction. counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a technical description of a near-eye display optical waveguide system in which an image propagates by four-fold reflection in a first guide, transfers to a second guide, then exits after two-fold reflection.
counterfactuals.output:
A near-eye display optical waveguide system includes an image source, an input coupling optic, a first optical guide, an inter-guide coupling region, a second optical guide, and an output coupling optic arranged to deliver an image-bearing beam toward an eyebox.

The image source, such as a microdisplay or scanning projector, emits image light that is collimated or partially collimated by projection optics. The input coupling optic injects the image light into the first optical guide at an angle satisfying total internal reflection conditions. The first optical guide is a transparent substrate, for example glass or optical polymer, having first and second major surfaces that define a propagation path.

Within the first optical guide, the image-bearing light propagates by four-fold reflection. In this configuration, a representative ray undergoes four successive reflections from the internal guide surfaces before reaching an inter-guide transfer region. The four-fold reflection path may be produced by total internal reflection at opposed major surfaces, by reflective coatings, by diffractive or holographic turning structures, or by a combination thereof. The four reflections fold the optical path within a compact substrate thickness while maintaining angular and spatial information corresponding to the image.

At the end of the four-reflection propagation path, the light is directed to an optical transfer element positioned between the first guide and a second optical guide. The transfer element may include a partially reflective interface, prism coupler, surface-relief grating, volume holographic grating, polarization-selective coating, or index-matched bonding layer. This element redirects or couples the image light out of the first guide and into the second guide while preserving the field angle distribution of the image.

The second optical guide is arranged adjacent to, parallel to, or optically bonded with the first guide. After transfer, the image light propagates in the second guide by two-fold reflection. A representative ray reflects twice from internal surfaces of the second guide before reaching an exit region. The two-fold reflection path further relays and positions the image light for extraction while enabling a compact near-eye form factor.

At the exit region, an output coupling optic extracts the image-bearing light from the second guide toward the viewer’s eye. The output coupler may be implemented as a reflective facet, diffractive grating, holographic optical element, beam-splitting coating, or polarization-dependent extractor. The extracted light forms an exit pupil or expanded eyebox at a designed eye relief distance.

The system may be configured so that the four-fold reflection in the first guide performs primary lateral transport or pupil expansion, while the two-fold reflection in the second guide performs final redirection, pupil replication, or image extraction. Optical coatings, guide thicknesses, refractive indices, and coupling angles are selected to maintain total internal reflection during guided propagation and to provide efficient transfer and controlled outcoupling at the designated regions. The resulting architecture provides a compact near-eye display waveguide capable of routing an image through a folded optical path before delivering it to the user’s eye.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe, in patent language, an aperture expansion system where image light enters a first elongated optical waveguide at an oblique angle, is partially reflected into a second waveguide, and is then emitted through a parallel face.
counterfactuals.output:
An aperture expansion system comprises a first elongated optical waveguide having a longitudinal axis and including an input region configured to receive image-bearing light at an oblique angle relative to a major surface of the first elongated optical waveguide. The first elongated optical waveguide is configured to guide the image-bearing light by total internal reflection along the longitudinal axis.

A partially reflective optical element is optically coupled to, embedded within, or disposed adjacent to the first elongated optical waveguide and is arranged to redirect at least a portion of the guided image-bearing light out of the first elongated optical waveguide and into a second optical waveguide. The partially reflective optical element may comprise a beam splitter, a semi-reflective coating, a transflective surface, or a plurality of spaced partially reflective surfaces configured to provide pupil or aperture expansion in a first direction.

The second optical waveguide is optically coupled to the first elongated optical waveguide and includes a pair of opposing, substantially parallel major faces. The second optical waveguide is configured to receive the redirected image-bearing light and to propagate the received light therein by internal reflection. One of the substantially parallel major faces of the second optical waveguide comprises an output face or is associated with an out-coupling structure configured to emit the image-bearing light from the second optical waveguide through the output face.

In operation, image light incident upon the first elongated optical waveguide at the oblique angle is coupled into the first elongated optical waveguide and propagated along the first elongated optical waveguide. A first portion of the image light is reflected by the partially reflective optical element toward the second optical waveguide, while another portion may continue propagation within the first elongated optical waveguide for subsequent reflection or extraction. The reflected portion enters the second optical waveguide and is emitted through the parallel output face thereof, thereby expanding an effective aperture of the image light.

In one embodiment, the first elongated optical waveguide provides aperture expansion in a first dimension and the second optical waveguide provides aperture expansion or output distribution in a second dimension. The system may be incorporated into a near-eye display, head-mounted display, projection display, or other optical apparatus requiring enlargement of an exit pupil or output aperture while maintaining a compact optical form factor.
